terminal_record.title: CBP's Electronic-Device Search Policy Predates the 2025 Claim
terminal_record.description_short: DHS announced electronic-media border-search directives in 2009; the record does not establish a February 2025 expansion.
terminal_record.description_medium: DHS announced directives governing searches of computers and other electronic media at U.S. ports of entry in August 2009. The eCFR separately defines “reasonable distance” for immigration officers as within 100 air miles of a U.S. external boundary, and a 2008 ACLU report traces that regulation to 1953. These sources establish a preexisting framework, not a February 2025 Trump action ending Fourth Amendment protections or expanding device searches. The claimed thousands of court challenges remain unsupported.
terminal_record.description_long: On August 27, 2009, the Department of Homeland Security announced directives for searches of computers and other electronic media at U.S. ports of entry. DHS described the policy as consistent with its border authority over non-electronic materials. Separately, the eCFR defines “reasonable distance” under section 287(a)(3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act as within 100 air miles from an external boundary, while a 2008 ACLU report says the regulation establishing the 100-mile zone was adopted in 1953. These sources show that electronic-media border-search guidance and the 100-mile immigration regulation predate the alleged February 2025 policy. They do not establish that Trump ended Fourth Amendment protections, expanded an electronic-device search zone in February 2025, or caused thousands of court challenges. The frozen entry also combines the statutory operating distance for immigration officers with electronic-device searches; the accessed material does not show that the two authorities are interchangeable. This replacement narrows the card to the documented policy background and leaves the claimed 2025 action unsupported.

source_fact_map.fact: DHS announced directives for searches of electronic media at U.S. ports of entry in 2009.
source_fact_map.quote: The new directives address the circumstances under which U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) can conduct border searches of electronic media
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The new directives address the circumstances under which U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) can conduct border searches of electronic media—consistent with the Department’s Constitutional authority to search other sensitive non-electronic materials, such as briefcases, backpacks and notebooks, at U.S. borders.

source_fact_map.fact: A 2008 ACLU report says the 100-mile border-zone regulation was adopted in 1953.
source_fact_map.quote: The regulations establishing the 100-mile border zone were adopted by the U.S. Department of Justice in 1953
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The regulations establishing the 100-mile border zone were adopted by the U.S. Department of Justice in 1953—without any public comments or debate. At the time, there were fewer than 1,100 Border Patrol agents nationwide; today, there are over 21,000.

source_fact_map.fact: The eCFR defines reasonable distance under INA section 287(a)(3) as within 100 air miles of an external boundary or a shorter distance set by officials.
source_fact_map.quote: means within 100 air miles from any external boundary of the United States or any shorter distance which may be fixed by the chief patrol agent for CBP
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The term reasonable distance, as used in section 287(a) (3) of the Act, means within 100 air miles from any external boundary of the United States or any shorter distance which may be fixed by the chief patrol agent for CBP, or the special agent in charge for ICE

uncertainties: No source accessed establishes a February 2025 action by Trump expanding electronic-device searches or ending Fourth Amendment protections.
The eCFR section addresses a statutory immigration-law distance; it does not itself establish a blanket authority to search every person or device within that zone.
The frozen statement that courts received thousands of challenges is unsupported and omitted.
The ACLU historical date is documented here from a search excerpt; its full page was not extracted.

The 100-mile border-zone regulation predates the claimed 2025 action; the 2008 ACLU report dates its adoption to 1953.
Current eCFR text defines the statutory reasonable-distance term as up to 100 air miles, with shorter distances available.
